title: Heavy Rain Lashes Banka as Monsoon Eases Bihar's Humid Heat - streamlinefeed.co.ke
full_text:
Heavy rain lashed Banka district on Friday, cooling streets that have sweltered through weeks of humid heat and filling dams along the monsoon-soaked east of Bihar.
The downpour, captured in footage circulated by IANS on August 21, arrives in a state that has spent the season oscillating between heat alerts and flood warnings, and it crystallises the double-edged bargain of the Indian monsoon.
Relief After a Sweltering Season
Banka's August days have peaked between 31 and 35 degrees Celsius with oppressive humidity, and AccuWeather's monthly track shows highs between 87 and 95 degrees Fahrenheit with overnight lows that never let the humidity break. The India Meteorological Department's long-range forecast warned in June of above-normal heatwave days across Bihar. The southwest monsoon entered the state on June 11, and each subsequent spell has been measured against two anxieties: will it break the heat, and will it breach the embankments?
Dams, Embankments and Orange Alerts
The Water Resources Department keeps a close vigil on all embankments, and the Badua dam in Banka district has filled to its brim after successive spells, footage from the department shows. IMD issued an orange alert for heavy to very heavy rain over Bihar in July, and forecast a vigorous monsoon spell over the state in the first week of August, with heavy rainfall flagged for Banka and neighbouring districts on August 5, 6 and 7.
- June 11: southwest monsoon enters Bihar.
- July: IMD orange alert for heavy to very heavy rain.
- Aug 5 to 7: heavy rainfall window flagged for Banka and neighbours.
- Aug 21: IANS footage shows heavy rain easing the humid heat.
The rain's violence is not abstract. Earlier this season, lightning strikes during thunderstorms in Banka killed five people, including a father and his seven-year-old son, local reports said, a reminder that monsoon mortality in Bihar is often electrical before it is aquatic.
The Flood Equation
Banka sits on the eastern plateau fringe, but its rivers feed the same basins that make Bihar India's most flood-exposed state, with a majority of its 38 districts prone to annual inundation, most famously along the Koshi. Every full dam is therefore both an asset for irrigation and a liability downstream, and the state's disaster machinery treats each August spell as a live drill.
A Monsoon With Global Echoes
The same Indian Ocean currents that drive these rains also shape East Africa's short rains, and a vigorous monsoon feeds global rice price signals that reach Kenyan importers within weeks. When Bihar floods, the Indian government restricts rice exports, and the grain shelves of Nairobi supermarkets feel the tremor.
For now, Banka is counting blessings in millimetres. The heat has broken, the dams are full, and the embankments, so far, are holding.
